title: Cost Estimation — Core Method
description: Every plan gets a price before it runs: the estimator combines index statistics — row counts, selectivity, page sizes — with a cost model for I/O and CPU. Estimates are relative, not absolute: the optimizer only needs to rank plans, not predict wall-clock time. Stale statistics produce bad estimates, so the estimator tracks stat freshness and distrusts ancient numbers. Cost estimation turns plan selection from guesswork into engineering. At ladder rank 1 this is the simple core: a single, self-contained application of the method.
demo:
stats = {"rows": 1000000, "index_pages": 2000}
def cost_scan(): return stats["rows"] / 1000
def cost_index(sel): return stats["index_pages"] * sel + 10
print("full scan cost:", cost_scan())
print("index cost (sel=0.01):", cost_index(0.01))

title: Index Selection — Core Method
description: Given a query's predicates, the optimizer lists candidate indexes and picks the one with the lowest estimated cost — usually the most selective predicate's index, but covering indexes that avoid table visits can win. Multi-column indexes are considered when predicates align with their column order. The choice is re-evaluated per query because data distribution shifts. Right index selection is the single biggest lever on query performance. At ladder rank 1 this is the simple core: a single, self-contained application of the method.

title: Join Ordering — Core Method
description: Joining three tables in the wrong order can turn milliseconds into hours, so the optimizer orders joins smallest-first using estimated cardinalities. Dynamic programming explores the plan space for complex queries, while greedy heuristics handle the simple ones fast. The cardinalities come from table statistics and predicate selectivity, chained through each join. Join ordering is the classic triumph of cost-based optimization. At ladder rank 1 this is the simple core: a single, self-contained application of the method.

title: Plan Comparison — Core Method
description: The optimizer never trusts a single plan: it enumerates candidates — different indexes, join orders, access paths — costs each one, and keeps the cheapest. Enumeration is pruned aggressively using the same cost model, so the search itself stays cheap. The winning plan is logged with its cost breakdown, making slow queries explainable after the fact. Enumerate, cost, pick: the optimizer's entire creed. At ladder rank 1 this is the simple core: a single, self-contained application of the method.
demo:
plans = {"seq_scan": 1200, "idx_scan": 45, "bitmap": 60}
best = min(plans, key=plans.get)
print("plans:", plans)
print("winner:", best, "cost", plans[best])

title: Selectivity Estimation — Core Method
description: Selectivity — the fraction of rows a predicate keeps — drives every cost estimate, and the optimizer derives it from histograms, most-common-value lists, and distinct counts. Equality on a uniform column selects 1/distinct; range predicates interpolate the histogram. When statistics are missing, the optimizer falls back to defaults and marks the estimate as low-confidence. Good selectivity estimates are the difference between a brilliant plan and a disastrous one. At ladder rank 1 this is the simple core: a single, self-contained application of the method.
demo:
distinct = 50
sel_eq = 1.0 / distinct
print("equality selectivity: %.3f" % sel_eq)
print("expected rows from 1M: %d" % int(1000000 * sel_eq))
